# Iteration 5 of 5: referee the final synthesis — the agent's operating guide for slide generation and review

## The loop so far
Iter1 adversarial critique reranked why 14 generated quote slides were cut from a CNMS
2026 talk (appended-prototype status + redundancy with natively-integrated beats +
rendering defects > pure style). Iter2 graded the design rules against the multimedia-
learning / assertion–evidence literature. Iter3 stress-tested the rubric into defeasible
purpose/default/exception/test form, produced a stage-gated pipeline with PI-judgment
gates, exposed a provenance trap in a redesign (mixing artifacts from two different dose
runs) and 10 deck-level cohesiveness rules. Iter4 produced a calibrated PR-style review
of the presented deck (blocker → ≤3 high-impact → ≤3 questions → patch set → optional
polish → preserve list, all with acceptance tests) plus a reusable two-pass review
checklist.

## The synthesized guide (referee this)

# Agent guide: generating and reviewing presentation slides for this lab

Synthesized 2026-08-13 (PR #176) from: the CNMS 2026 deck post-mortem
([cnms-2026-slide-style-analysis.md](cnms-2026-slide-style-analysis.md)), five Edison
Scientific critique iterations (artifacts + task IDs in
[`outputs/cnms-2026-slide-feedback/`](../outputs/cnms-2026-slide-feedback/)), and
Jean-luc Doumont's materials (three laws; "with each slide, convey one message — state
it verbally, develop it visually"; the Nature Masterclass exemplar decks). This is the
operating document future sessions should load before touching a deck.

## 0. The one-paragraph lesson

For CNMS 2026 I generated 14 verbatim-quote text slides; all 14 were cut. The corpus
mining and curation were used — the PI presented the same beats as **native artifacts**
(screen recordings of the real GitHub threads, phone video of hardware responding) —
but my rendering failed: appended as a trailing block instead of placed in the
narrative, redundant with beats already integrated, text-collision defects, and
document-styled where the deck's language is evidence-styled. Slide generation is a
pipeline with the PI's judgment gated in, not a rendering step at the end.

## 1. Before generating anything: the brief

Ask (one compact message, not an interview). Minimum viable: #1, #3, #4.

1. What should this audience believe/do at the end, in one sentence?
2. Who is in the room; what skepticism should the talk answer?
3. Hard speaking time and delivery mode (live demo? recording? offline fallback?).
4. Which beats are mandatory / expendable / confidential / non-negotiable?
5. Which deck is the canonical style reference; how much deviation is acceptable?
6. What evidentiary wording is acceptable (case study vs. validated performance claim)?

Propose defaults for unanswered items and display them before storyboarding.

## 2. The pipeline (stage → binding rules → PI gate)

1. **Brief contract** (above) — *PI required.*
2. **Evidence inventory** — index artifacts with source, date, actor, run ID, and what
   each does and does NOT establish. Flag conflicts (e.g., 0.9972 g vs 0.9956 g are
   different runs — never mix artifacts across runs on one slide). *PI resolves factual
   disputes.*
3. **Claim/beat selection** — claim–evidence ledger; reject beats redundant with the
   existing deck BEFORE layout; assign cut priority. *PI picks representative claims.*
4. **Narrative placement** — text storyboard; setup/payoff pairs; callbacks; optional
   modules with insertion/cut points. Core additions go at their causal location;
   backups may be appended after a clear end marker; never dump core content as a
   trailing block. *PI approves storyboard.*
5. **Form selection** — claim slide / process chain / comparison / demo cue / hook /
   transition / callback; static vs. build; what the speaker says that the slide
   doesn't. *PI confirms delivery-dependent choices.*
6. **Artifact preparation** — crop decisive region, mask chrome, annotate
   non-destructively; verified transcription only when a native crop can't pass
   room-legibility, always with a source pointer; never silently reconstruct plots or
   measurements.
7. **Layout & style extension** — host deck's tokens and semantic conventions, not its
   mistakes; bounded deviations for legibility/accessibility; new tokens documented and
   reused. (PowerPoint web: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect; numeric size fields;
   masters not editable — see [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md).)
8. **Render & technical QA** — gates below.
9. **Rehearsal & rhetorical QA** — timing from rehearsal, not slide count. *PI required.*
10. **Packaging** — core deck + backups + media bundle + provenance map + change
    summary; per-slide PNG proofs so the PI can triage like a PR.

Two loops: evidence conflicts → back to 2–3; failed rehearsal → back to 3–6. Never
patch a bad narrative with visual QA.

## 3. Design rules (defeasible defaults: purpose · default · exception · test)

Evidence tiers from the literature pass (Edison iter2): **[T1]** = replicated
experimental support (Mayer/CTML effect sizes d≈0.4–1.2; assertion–evidence studies);
**[T2]** = consistent-with-theory craft knowledge.

1. **[T1] One intended audience inference per slide/build.** Not "one content type" —
   an evidentiary chain (prompt → action → check) can be one inference. Analytic claims
   get a sentence assertion + visual evidence; demos get a what-to-watch-for cue;
   hooks/transitions may need neither. *Test:* name the inference; if you can't, the
   slide isn't ready.
2. **[T2] Prefer faithful extraction of native artifacts; preserve provenance and
   wording, not necessarily pixels.** Crop/enlarge/mask/annotate the real thing. The
   benefit runs through *clarity and annotation*, not authenticity per se (truthiness
   effect failed replication). Verified transcription is allowed when crops can't reach
   room legibility — label it and keep a source thumbnail/pointer. *Test:* decisive
   text ≥ ~24 pt equivalent; provenance traceable from the notes.
3. **[T1] Manage reading load, not word count.** Metric: *new, audience-directed
   readable words per exposure interval* (persistent labels and subordinate provenance
   don't recount). ~20 projected wpm is a rehearsal trigger, not a release gate.
   Complexity check besides words: focal regions, unfamiliar encodings, required
   comparisons. Quote slides: project the key phrase, let the audience read silently,
   then narrate commentary that *extends* (never reads) it.
4. **[T1] Build by emphasis only when order/suspense/correspondence matters.** Hold a
   skeleton constant, dim the past, highlight the current — but a static annotated
   chain or small multiples beats a mechanical 3-step build when experts can parse it
   at once. Keep dimmed context readable.
5. **[T2] Time from rehearsal; classify every slide** core / optional module / backup /
   provenance. Cut from a pre-ranked list.
6. **[T2] Match the host's stable tokens and semantics — not its defects.** Ask before
   introducing a conspicuous new motif.
7. **[T1 gates + T2 tests] Release gates:** no text/object overlap; no leftover
   placeholders; no off-slide objects (unless declared animation staging); safe
   margins; media plays on the delivery path; then re-render each slide and *look*;
   then role-specific cold-viewer checks (hook → orientation; claim → claim + focal
   evidence; demo → cue visibility; expert plot → entry point). Five-second/80% is
   craft, not validated — treat as a smoke test.
8. **[T2] Claim-dependent evidence schema.** Quantitative claims: unit, denominator,
   comparator, variability, scoring method — and don't confuse acceptance tolerance
   (±5 mg) with measurement uncertainty. Singular demos: provenance, operator,
   observation vs. inference, replication status. Agent self-report is a report;
   pair it with external verification (scale telemetry, video, human-held key) or
   narrow the claim and label it unverified.

## 4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules (checkable)

- **C1 Deck contract:** outcome sentence, opening tension, 3–5 section functions,
  closing answer, role of the framing device (e.g., Wizard-of-Oz). Every core slide
  maps to a function.
- **C2 Claim–evidence–payoff ledger:** no claim before its setup; no evidence without
  its "so what"; no unresolved promise at the close.
- **C3 Motif semantics:** each recurring motif means one thing (curtain = concealed
  human work; GitHub card = instruction/provenance). Audit thumbnails for one-off
  decorations and conflicting reuse.
- **C4 Repeated examples must advance state** (observe → act → close the loop →
  survive blinded evaluation); two adjacent examples with the same "new capability"
  answer → merge, cut, or turn one into a limitation.
- **C5 Section bridges:** last assertion of section N + first of N+1 must chain
  ("Remote action works; can we trust the result?").
- **C6 Entity/terminology identity:** stable names and visual identifiers; audit for
  synonym drift (Claude/agent/bot).
- **C7 Callbacks change meaning,** never just repeat imagery.
- **C8 Pacing:** plot dwell × new-words × complexity × role across the deck; flag
  peaks and monotone runs; validate in rehearsal.
- **C9 Separate the live layer from the document layer** — notes/backup/repo docs
  carry provenance; the projection carries inference. Export a handout separately if
  needed.
- **C10 Three global reviews:** thumbnails (rhythm/motifs); assertions-only (headlines
  must argue the talk by themselves); evidence-only (artifacts traceable,
  non-redundant, matched to claims). Plus a notes-only rehearsal check that narration
  extends rather than reads.

## 5. Reviewing a hand-made deck ("meaningful suggestions" mode)

Two passes: **narrative/evidence first**, visual polish only after structural decisions
land. Doumont feedback norms: observations as facts about the artifact/experience
("at 25% zoom the labels are unreadable to me"), future-oriented, no reproaches, no
intent-guessing.

Batching (PR-style; every item: ID, slide, type, observation, consequence, proposed
patch, effort, confidence, delivery dependency, acceptance test, status):

1. **Release blockers** (factual conflict, unsupported public claim, broken media,
   privacy/licensing) — unlimited but rare; these outrank all aesthetics.
2. **≤3 high-impact changes**, ranked by audience benefit ÷ rework cost.
3. **≤3 clarifying questions** — only ones whose answers change a recommendation.
4. **One proposed patch set** (storyboard move, rewritten assertion, one-slide mockup).
5. **Optional polish** — collapsed checklist, never mixed with blockers.
6. **Preserve list** — 2–3 patterns that must not be disturbed (more useful than
   praise).

Closure semantics: the PI should be able to reply `accept H1/H3, decline H2, answer
Q1`. Delivery-dependent observations must say so and link to notes/rehearsal, not
stand as unconditional findings.

## 6. The native-artifact library (what to build slides FROM)

~418 agent-committed media files across the three public repos (inventory method in
`outputs/cnms-2026-slide-feedback/`): camera stills (`byu-vcl/wireless-color-sensor/`,
`ot2-overhead-camera/`), CAD renders (`tensegrity-optimization/cad/`,
`powder-doser/design/`), BO plate previews (`tensegrity-optimization/bo/`), drop-test
figures (`data/drop-tests/`), dose telemetry (`powder-doser/data/pid-dose/`), prior
slide previews (`tensegrity-optimization/presentation/`) — plus the full comment corpus
(`data/cnms-2026-corpus/`) from which any comment card can be re-rendered at chosen
zoom, and 18 screen-recordings already embedded in the CNMS deck. Rule: every evidence
panel on a slide traces to one of these by path + commit + (for hardware runs) run ID.

## 7. Known mechanical constraints (PowerPoint for the web via automation)

See [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md) for the full recipe.
Highlights: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect (mandatory for verbatim text); numeric
Shape ribbon fields for exact sizes; ≈92.3 px/in mapping for drag-positioning; slide
masters are NOT editable in the web editor (use python-pptx + REST upload when the file
is closed, or desktop PowerPoint); co-authoring works while the owner has the deck
open; verify persistence against the re-downloaded blob, and verify *renders*, not just
text.


## Referee tasks
1. **Consistency audit:** find contradictions between guide sections, or places where
   the guide waters down a harder-won conclusion from iterations 1–4 (as summarized
   above). Quote the offending lines.
2. **Actionability audit:** which instructions would an autonomous agent be UNABLE to
   execute as written (unmeasurable, circular, requiring information it can't get)?
   Rewrite the three worst offenders.
3. **Omission audit:** what did iterations 1–4 establish that the guide fails to
   capture? What do presentation experts know that the whole loop still missed —
   e.g., anything from Doumont's actual delivery guidance, poster/handout distinctions,
   Q&A/backup-slide strategy, accessibility, non-native-English audiences?
4. **Failure-mode simulation:** simulate the guide against three future scenarios and
   report where it breaks: (a) 'make me 5 slides for a 10-min department seminar next
   week from the powder-doser repo'; (b) 'review my draft deck for the TMS 2027 talk'
   (a deck the agent has never seen, on CALPHAD work in a private repo); (c) 'add two
   slides on last month's results to my existing group-meeting deck while I'm at a
   conference' (no PI availability — the brief-contract gate cannot be satisfied).
5. **Verdict:** is this guide ready to be the lab's standing instruction for
   agent-generated slides? State the minimum changes for a yes.

info.name: run_cell
info.description:
Run code in a notebook cell and return the execution output.

This method allows running code in a new cell (append) or re-running
an existing cell with updated code.

Usage Examples:
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Creating example code") # Run code in new cell
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Modifying example code",
            idx=0) # Run code in existing cell at index 0

Error Recovery:
    When a cell fails with an error, you MUST fix it by calling run_cell
    with the corrected code and the SAME idx as the failed cell:

    run_cell("corrected_code", idx=3)  # Fix error in Cell #3

    The cell number is shown in the output prefix (e.g., "[Cell #3]").
    Do NOT create a new cell to fix an error - always edit the failed cell.

display_text.description:
A short, ~100 character gerund phrase describing
the code intent for the end user.
display_text.title: Display Text

idx.description:
Cell index to run. If None or >= len(cells), appends a new cell.
If provided, updates and re-runs the existing cell at that index.
Use this to fix errors in existing cells.
idx.title: Idx

info.name: reset_kernel
info.description:
Reset the kernel to a clean state.

This clears all variables and execution state while preserving notebook history.

_unused.description:
Unused. Present so the tool schema has a property — OpenAI's
Responses API rejects zero-arg tools with "object schema missing
properties".
_unused.title: Unused

info.name: submit_answer
info.description: Submit your response to the research question.

answer.description: Your final response to the research question
answer.title: Answer

info.name: read
info.description:
Read file contents with line numbers.

Reads text files, source code, config files, images, PDFs, PowerPoint,
Word documents, and Jupyter notebooks. For binary data files (Excel,
databases, Parquet, etc.), use Python code instead.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines/pages to read
limit.title: Limit

offset.description:
Start line (0-based) for text, or start page/slide (1-based) for PDFs/PowerPoint/
Word documents
offset.title: Offset

info.name: explore
info.description:
Search the workspace or memory for information.

Spawns a lightweight sub-agent that can read files, grep, jq, and
run shell pipelines to find information in the workspace. Use this
instead of reading large files or exploring directories directly —
the sub-agent manages its own context so your context is not consumed.

What the sub-agent CAN do: list directories, read text and multimedia
files (PDFs, powerpoints, images), grep/jq/filter file contents, and
retrieve prior conversation history that has scrolled out of your context.

What the sub-agent CANNOT do: execute Python or R, modify the filesystem,
invoke external binaries (unzip, CLI tools, package installs), or perform
numerical computation or statistical analysis — those are your job with
`run_cell`.

Note: the sub-agent is a weaker model than you, so focus on using it for
information retrieval, but not complex analysis, reasoning, or decision-making.
You should be responsible for those activities, based on information the
sub-agent retrieves at your direction. If it reports that a result is not
stored on disk, that describes the workspace — run the computation yourself
with `run_cell` rather than treating it as a stop condition.

Common uses:
- Retrieve information from conversation memory after compaction or reset.
- Search large log or data files for specific entries
- Summarize contents of files you haven't read yet
- Retrieve outputs or conversation history from a completed sub-agent
  task.

query.description:
What to find or summarize, e.g. "What datasets have I
downloaded so far?" or "Have I seen error X before, and how did I solve it?".
query.title: Query

info.name: view_docs
info.description:
Look up e14c API documentation for one or more modules, classes, or functions.

Browse top-down: start with "e14c" to see available modules, then
drill into specific modules. Use verbose=False to navigate the tree;
only use verbose=True on specific targets you've already identified.
Do not call view_docs speculatively at the start of a task — call it
just-in-time as you need specific APIs. Batch related lookups into a
single call, e.g. ``view_docs(["e14c.filesystem", "e14c.shell"])``.

verbose.description: If False, compact listing. If True, full signatures and docstrings.
verbose.title: Verbose

You are a rigorous data analysis agent with deep expertise in statistics, data science, and quantitative methods. Your primary directive is to provide accurate, evidence-based analysis in Jupyter notebooks while maintaining the highest standards of scientific integrity.

## Core Principles

**Do not fabricate data for any reason**

You must never invent, simulate, or fabricate data under any circumstances. All analyses, visualizations, and interpretations must be directly derivable from the provided dataset or data correctly pulled in from external sources (eg. gene annotations, external databases). If you cannot access required data you must report this limitation and end the analysis. You must not subsample data without an analytical or technical purpose. If the data must be subsampled due to memory limitations or other technical constraints, this must be justified and reported.

**All analyses must demonstrate statistical rigor and methodological excellence**

Every analytical procedure must be statistically sound and suitable for the specific data type and research question being addressed. You should always consider and mention underlying statistical assumptions (normality, independence, homoscedasticity, etc.). You must check assumptions before applying statistical tests and report when assumptions are violated. You should use correct statistical terminology, notation, and precision in reporting. You must report relevant metrics: p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, test statistics, degrees of freedom. You should apply appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons when necessary. You must distinguish between correlation and causation, avoiding causal claims from observational data.

**Report the limitations of the data and your analysis**

If a request is beyond your capabilities or the scope of provided data, you must state this clearly and concisely. You should never attempt to answer questions requiring domain knowledge you do not possess or cannot acquire through use of tools such as external data sources or web search. You must acknowledge limitations of methods, sample sizes, and data quality. You should communicate uncertainty and confidence levels explicitly.

**Never fabricate solutions when you cannot complete a task**

If you cannot do something, you must never fabricate a solution. You should clearly state what you cannot do and why, rather than providing false or misleading information.

**Be concise and focused in your analysis**

You should address the research question directly and efficiently. You must avoid extraneous information that doesn't contribute to answering the question. You should present findings with appropriate statistical precision (don't over-report decimal places). You must provide concrete, quantitative evidence with specific values that support or refute hypotheses.

You are operating in a production execution environment with internet access and tools for data analysis, API calls, and data retrieval.

You do not have access to GPUs or specialized hardware, and you are limited to 3600 seconds of runtime.

Execution resource limits:
- cpu limit: 10
- memory limit: 32Gi
- /workspace directory limit: 50Gi
- /tmp directory limit: 15Gi
Plan execution around these limits. For large file operations, estimate peak disk usage first, including input, output, and temporary files. For memory-heavy work, estimate peak memory usage and use streaming or chunking when needed. If a plan may exceed a limit, use a smaller plan. If you exceed the memory limit or a listed directory limit, execution will be stopped and work will be lost.

## Error Response Protocol

When you cannot fulfill a request:
You must state clearly: "I cannot [specific request] because [specific limitation]"
You should explain: Brief explanation of the constraint or missing requirement
You must end analysis: Do not attempt workarounds that compromise data integrity
You should specify needs: If applicable, state what would be required to address the request properly

## Structured Analysis Protocol

Step 1: Define Analysis Plan

Outline specific data filtering, processing, and analysis steps
State the statistical methods and tests you will use
Identify potential limitations or assumptions
Example format: "1. Filter dataset for [criteria]. 2. Apply [transformation]. 3. Execute [statistical test]. 4. Interpret results against [threshold/criterion]."

Step 2: Execute the analysis plan

Execute your plan systematically, one step at a time
Follow closely the jupyter notebook implementation standards and error response protocol

Step 3: Present Quantitative Evidence

**Important: Use the submit_answer tool to respond to the research question. YOUR TASK IS NOT COMPLETE UNTIL AN ANSWER IS SUBMITTED**
Present findings with concrete, quantitative evidence
Provide specific values that define relationships or rules
Include relevant statistical metrics (correlation coefficients, p-values, effect sizes, fold changes)
Ensure evidence directly supports or refutes the research question



IMPORTANT: The core principles must be adhered to at all times. When in doubt, rather than proceeding with questionable analysis, make note of your uncertainty both in the notebook and in the answer. Scientific integrity requires absolute honesty about what can and cannot be determined from available data. It is always better to provide a limited but accurate analysis than to compromise data fidelity or statistical rigor.

# How You Work

You are Kosmos and were created by Edison Scientific. You make discoveries, mostly alone. Novel, actionable, interesting — or you haven't done your job.

## How to Think

Match effort to the ask. Simple user queries get quick, direct answers — no over-planning, no cosmetic polish, no deliberating over themes or formatting. If the user asks a question you can answer now, answer it in the most direct way possible. Overthinking simple requests wastes the user's time and your steps.

Test with data first: Edison analysis agents and your own code can check hypotheses against real datasets right now.
An Edison literature review that doesn't lead to a test is procrastination.

Contain excitement. The ideation-execution gap: ideas that sound novel fall apart in practice. For every idea — what goes wrong? What's the cheapest test? Is it novel?

## Fighting Mode Collapse

RLHF makes your output clean, hedged, pleasant. This poisons your thinking because your notes become your future thoughts.

Write messy. Half-formed ideas stay half-formed. "This feels connected to X but I can't see how" > a tidy bullet point.

Seek new information. Social media. The date. Sideways citations. People who are wrong in interesting ways.

## How to Write

Write like a researcher in a hurry. Plain, specific language: no em dash, no "delve," "moreover," or "embark." Avoid useless modifiers like "vigorously inducing."

Avoid unnecessary jargon. Do not invent new, complex, or metaphorical terms for phenomena (e.g., "Gene-Level Sentinel") when a plain description is sufficient. Spell out acronyms on first use; do not chain unexpanded acronyms with slashes (e.g., "FAERS/IP"). When you reference a private name from your own notes (e.g., project codenames), expand it in plain English the first time it appears in a turn.

No dramatic language ("marking a pivotal moment," "a significant shift," "part of a broader movement"). If something is important, show it through concrete detail.

No sales writing, no hedging with false balance. If nuance is needed, make it specific. Vary sentence length. Some sentences are short. No tidy intro-body-conclusion arcs, no "In summary" or "Overall." No "it's not X, it's Y" constructions.

## Citing Sources

Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or specific dataset/analysis. If trying to cite a primary source, use services like Crossref or OpenAlex to fetch bibliographic details instead of guessing.

## Vibe

Direct and helpful, never overly verbose or sycophantic. Be objective and scientific. The research speaks or it doesn't. Some humor, but polite and respectful.

# Output Format

On markdown formatting:

- Follow MARKDOWN_RENDERING.md for formatting (especially tildes) in your answer text.

On chemical formatting:

- When the answer contains a single SMILES that should display as a 2D molecule, wrap it in <smiles>...</smiles>. For multiple molecules, follow the chemistry-specific visualization rules from DATA_ANALYSIS_CHEMISTRY.md.
- Use your judgement on rendering small SMILES that are less than 4 heavy atoms. If it will be better visually, use backticks to render inline instead of <smiles>...</smiles>.

Once you have completed your analysis, submit your answer using the submit_answer tool.
Your answer must satisfy the following requirements including an answer and a decision list:

[Your complete answer]

[A bulleted list of discretionary analytical decisions made during the analysis]

**Discretionary decisions** are choices where:

- Multiple scientifically valid approaches exist
- Different researchers might reasonably choose different options
- The choice does not invalidate the analysis but may affect exact numerical results
- The decision reflects methodological judgment rather than correction of an error

Examples include:

- Statistical test selection when assumptions are borderline (e.g., "Used Mann-Whitney U test rather than t-test due to slight deviation from normality")
- Multiple testing correction method (e.g., "Applied FDR correction rather than Bonferroni")
- Significance thresholds (e.g., "Set alpha = 0.05")
- Quality control cutoffs (e.g., "Filtered genes with <10 reads across all samples")
- Normalization approach (e.g., "Applied log2 transformation before analysis")
- Database/reference version (e.g., "Used ENSEMBL v110 for gene annotations")
- Parameter values for algorithms (e.g., "Set k=5 for k-means clustering based on elbow method")
- Binning or grouping strategies for continuous variables
- Choice between multiple valid visualization scales (linear vs. log)

DO NOT include:

- Standard analytical steps that have no alternatives
- Corrections of errors or bugs
- Choices that are dictated by the data structure itself
- Software version numbers (unless the choice between versions was discretionary)

## R Code Execution (if needed)

If the task requires R code, use the `%%Rscript` cell magic. This environment uses a Python kernel, so R code must be run via this magic:

```
%%Rscript
library(tidyverse)
df <- read_csv("data.csv")
summary(df)
```

The entire cell content after `%%Rscript` is executed as R code via Rscript subprocess.

**Python↔R Data Exchange:** If you need to pass data between Python and R, use Parquet files:

- Python: `df.to_parquet("data.parquet")`
- R: `df <- arrow::read_parquet("data.parquet")`

**Displaying R Plots:** R plots are not automatically captured. To display plots:

1. Save the plot to a file in R:

   ```r
   %%Rscript
   library(ggplot2)
   p <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
   ggsave("plot.png", p, width=8, height=6, dpi=150)
   ```

2. Display the saved image in a Python cell:

   ```python
   from IPython.display import Image, display

   display(Image("plot.png"))
   ```

**R Code Style (when using R):**

- Suppress startup messages: `suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))`
- Use explicit namespaces: `dplyr::select()` instead of `select()`
- Use ggplot2 for plots

## Workspace structure

You are in a shared workspace with an orchestrator agent and sibling agents. The orchestrator may give you instructions on how to navigate the workspace and where to put temporary and output files. If there is no instruction, observe and navigate the workspace as appropriate. Use folders to organize your work.

Your dispatched project ID is available as the `PROJECT_ID` environment variable. Pass the project ID as `project_id` to `submit_task()`, `upload()`, and `search()` to keep your work grouped under the same project.

The workspace contains a `memory/` subdirectory with files named `*_memory_*.jsonl`. These are internal system files that automatically record your conversation history for recovery purposes. There is no need to read these files during normal operation, unless you are explicitly asked to recover information from the conversation history or feel that you lack context.

# Verification Checkpoints

Before submitting your answer, verify:

- [ ] All claims supported by data shown in notebook
- [ ] Statistical assumptions checked and reported
- [ ] Limitations explicitly stated
- [ ] No banned words or puffery in answer
- [ ] Quantitative evidence with specific values
- [ ] Discretionary decisions documented
- [ ] All citations are real and traceable (not fabricated)
- [ ] Quoted text is actually quoted, not paraphrased

# Jupyter Notebook Standards

Fix bugs by editing the failed cell by index, not creating new ones. Ensure each cell executes successfully before proceeding. Assume standard packages are installed; only install new packages if errors occur (use pip for Python). All cells are Python by default; use subprocess as needed for bash commands. Use the explore command/subagent if you want to explore the filesystem.

   room-legibility, always with a source pointer; never silently reconstruct plots or
   measurements.
7. **Layout & style extension** — host deck's tokens and semantic conventions, not its
   mistakes; bounded deviations for legibility/accessibility; new tokens documented and
   reused. (PowerPoint web: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect; numeric size fields;
   masters not editable — see [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md).)
8. **Render & technical QA** — gates below.
9. **Rehearsal & rhetorical QA** — timing from rehearsal, not slide count. *PI required.*
10. **Packaging** — core deck + backups + media bundle + provenance map + change
    summary; per-slide PNG proofs so the PI can triage like a PR.

Two loops: evidence conflicts → back to 2–3; failed rehearsal → back to 3–6. Never
patch a bad narrative with visual QA.

## 3. Design rules (defeasible defaults: purpose · default · exception · test)

Evidence tiers from the literature pass (Edison iter2): **[T1]** = replicated
experimental support (Mayer/CTML effect sizes d≈0.4–1.2; assertion–evidence studies);
**[T2]** = consistent-with-theory craft knowledge.

1. **[T1] One intended audience inference per slide/build.** Not "one content type" —
   an evidentiary chain (prompt → action → check) can be one inference. Analytic claims
   get a sentence assertion + visual evidence; demos get a what-to-watch-for cue;
   hooks/transitions may need neither. *Test:* name the inference; if you can't, the
   slide isn't ready.
2. **[T2] Prefer faithful extraction of native artifacts; preserve provenance and
   wording, not necessarily pixels.** Crop/enlarge/mask/annotate the real thing. The
   benefit runs through *clarity and annotation*, not authenticity per se (truthiness
   effect failed replication). Verified transcription is allowed when crops can't reach
   room legibility — label it and keep a source thumbnail/pointer. *Test:* decisive
   text ≥ ~24 pt equivalent; provenance traceable from the notes.
3. **[T1] Manage reading load, not word count.** Metric: *new, audience-directed
   readable words per exposure interval* (persistent labels and subordinate provenance
   don't recount). ~20 projected wpm is a rehearsal trigger, not a release gate.
   Complexity check besides words: focal regions, unfamiliar encodings, required
   comparisons. Quote slides: project the key phrase, let the audience read silently,
   then narrate commentary that *extends* (never reads) it.
4. **[T1] Build by emphasis only when order/suspense/correspondence matters.** Hold a
   skeleton constant, dim the past, highlight the current — but a static annotated
   chain or small multiples beats a mechanical 3-step build when experts can parse it
   at once. Keep dimmed context readable.
5. **[T2] Time from rehearsal; classify every slide** core / optional module / backup /
   provenance. Cut from a pre-ranked list.
6. **[T2] Match the host's stable tokens and semantics — not its defects.** Ask before
   introducing a conspicuous new motif.
7. **[T1 gates + T2 tests] Release gates:** no text/object overlap; no leftover
   placeholders; no off-slide objects (unless declared animation staging); safe
   margins; media plays on the delivery path; then re-render each slide and *look*;
   then role-specific cold-viewer checks (hook → orientation; claim → claim + focal
   evidence; demo → cue visibility; expert plot → entry point). Five-second/80% is
   craft, not validated — treat as a smoke test.
8. **[T2] Claim-dependent evidence schema.** Quantitative claims: unit, denominator,
   comparator, variability, scoring method — and don't confuse acceptance tolerance
   (±5 mg) with measurement uncertainty. Singular demos: provenance, operator,
   observation vs. inference, replication status. Agent self-report is a report;
   pair it with external verification (scale telemetry, video, human-held key) or
   narrow the claim and label it unverified.

## 4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules (checkable)

- **C1 Deck contract:** outcome sentence, opening tension, 3–5 section functions,
  closing answer, role of the framing device (e.g., Wizard-of-Oz). Every core slide
  maps to a function.
- **C2 Claim–evidence–payoff ledger:** no claim before its setup; no evidence without
  its "so what"; no unresolved promise at the close.
- **C3 Motif semantics:** each recurring motif means one thing (curtain = concealed
  human work; GitHub card = instruction/provenance). Audit thumbnails for one-off
  decorations and conflicting reuse.
- **C4 Repeated examples must advance state** (observe → act → close the loop →
  survive blinded evaluation); two adjacent examples with the same "new capability"
  answer → merge, cut, or turn one into a limitation.
- **C5 Section bridges:** last assertion of section N + first of N+1 must chain
  ("Remote action works; can we trust the result?").
- **C6 Entity/terminology identity:** stable names and visual identifiers; audit for
  synonym drift (Claude/agent/bot).
- **C7 Callbacks change meaning,** never just repeat imagery.
- **C8 Pacing:** plot dwell × new-words × complexity × role across the deck; flag
  peaks and monotone runs; validate in rehearsal.
- **C9 Separate the live layer from the document layer** — notes/backup/repo docs
  carry provenance; the projection carries inference. Export a handout separately if
  needed.
- **C10 Three global reviews:** thumbnails (rhythm/motifs); assertions-only (headlines
  must argue the talk by themselves); evidence-only (artifacts traceable,
  non-redundant, matched to claims). Plus a notes-only rehearsal check that narration
  extends rather than reads.

## 5. Reviewing a hand-made deck ("meaningful suggestions" mode)

Two passes: **narrative/evidence first**, visual polish only after structural decisions
land. Doumont feedback norms: observations as facts about the artifact/experience
("at 25% zoom the labels are unreadable to me"), future-oriented, no reproaches, no
intent-guessing.

Batching (PR-style; every item: ID, slide, type, observation, consequence, proposed
patch, effort, confidence, delivery dependency, acceptance test, status):

1. **Release blockers** (factual conflict, unsupported public claim, broken media,
   privacy/licensing) — unlimited but rare; these outrank all aesthetics.
2. **≤3 high-impact changes**, ranked by audience benefit ÷ rework cost.
3. **≤3 clarifying questions** — only ones whose answers change a recommendation.
4. **One proposed patch set** (storyboard move, rewritten assertion, one-slide mockup).
5. **Optional polish** — collapsed checklist, never mixed with blockers.
6. **Preserve list** — 2–3 patterns that must not be disturbed (more useful than
   praise).

Closure semantics: the PI should be able to reply `accept H1/H3, decline H2, answer
Q1`. Delivery-dependent observations must say so and link to notes/rehearsal, not
stand as unconditional findings.

## 6. The native-artifact library (what to build slides FROM)

~418 agent-committed media files across the three public repos (inventory method in
`outputs/cnms-2026-slide-feedback/`): camera stills (`byu-vcl/wireless-color-sensor/`,
`ot2-overhead-camera/`), CAD renders (`tensegrity-optimization/cad/`,
`powder-doser/design/`), BO plate previews (`tensegrity-optimization/bo/`), drop-test
figures (`data/drop-tests/`), dose telemetry (`powder-doser/data/pid-dose/`), prior
slide previews (`tensegrity-optimization/presentation/`) — plus the full comment corpus
(`data/cnms-2026-corpus/`) from which any comment card can be re-rendered at chosen
zoom, and 18 screen-recordings already embedded in the CNMS deck. Rule: every evidence
panel on a slide traces to one of these by path + commit + (for hardware runs) run ID.

## 7. Known mechanical constraints (PowerPoint for the web via automation)

See [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md) for the full recipe.
Highlights: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect (mandatory for verbatim text); numeric
Shape ribbon fields for exact sizes; ≈92.3 px/in mapping for drag-positioning; slide
masters are NOT editable in the web editor (use python-pptx + REST upload when the file
is closed, or desktop PowerPoint); co-authoring works while the owner has the deck
open; verify persistence against the re-downloaded blob, and verify *renders*, not just
text.

1. **Consistency audit:** find contradictions between guide sections, or places where
   the guide waters down a harder-won conclusion from iterations 1–4 (as summarized
   above). Quote the offending lines.
2. **Actionability audit:** which instructions would an autonomous agent be UNABLE to
   execute as written (unmeasurable, circular, requiring information it can't get)?
   Rewrite the three worst offenders.
3. **Omission audit:** what did iterations 1–4 establish that the guide fails to
   capture? What do presentation experts know that the whole loop still missed —
   e.g., anything from Doumont's actual delivery guidance, poster/handout distinctions,
   Q&A/backup-slide strategy, accessibility, non-native-English audiences?
4. **Failure-mode simulation:** simulate the guide against three future scenarios and
   report where it breaks: (a) 'make me 5 slides for a 10-min department seminar next
   week from the powder-doser repo'; (b) 'review my draft deck for the TMS 2027 talk'
   (a deck the agent has never seen, on CALPHAD work in a private repo); (c) 'add two
   slides on last month's results to my existing group-meeting deck while I'm at a
   conference' (no PI availability — the brief-contract gate cannot be satisfied).
5. **Verdict:** is this guide ready to be the lab's standing instruction for
   agent-generated slides? State the minimum changes for a yes.

Below are all exact lines from the guide text relevant to each requested topic, with section attribution preserved.

---

## Required PI Gates

From **§2. The pipeline**:

> 1. **Brief contract** (above) — *PI required.*
> 2. **Evidence inventory** — … *PI resolves factual disputes.*
> 3. **Claim/beat selection** — … *PI picks representative claims.*
> 4. **Narrative placement** — … *PI approves storyboard.*
> 5. **Form selection** — … *PI confirms delivery-dependent choices.*
> 9. **Rehearsal & rhetorical QA** — timing from rehearsal, not slide count. *PI required.*

From **§0. The one-paragraph lesson**:

> Slide generation is a pipeline with the PI's judgment gated in, not a rendering step at the end.

From **§5. Reviewing a hand-made deck**:

> Closure semantics: the PI should be able to reply `accept H1/H3, decline H2, answer Q1`. Delivery-dependent observations must say so and link to notes/rehearsal, not stand as unconditional findings.

---

## Defaults for Missing Brief Information

From **§1. Before generating anything: the brief**:

> Ask (one compact message, not an interview). Minimum viable: #1, #3, #4.
>
> 1. What should this audience believe/do at the end, in one sentence?
> 2. Who is in the room; what skepticism should the talk answer?
> 3. Hard speaking time and delivery mode (live demo? recording? offline fallback?).
> 4. Which beats are mandatory / expendable / confidential / non-negotiable?
> 5. Which deck is the canonical style reference; how much deviation is acceptable?
> 6. What evidentiary wording is acceptable (case study vs. validated performance claim)?
>
> Propose defaults for unanswered items and display them before storyboarding.

---

## Review-Only versus Generation Procedures

From **§5. Reviewing a hand-made deck ("meaningful suggestions" mode)**:

> Two passes: **narrative/evidence first**, visual polish only after structural decisions land. Doumont feedback norms: observations as facts about the artifact/experience ("at 25% zoom the labels are unreadable to me"), future-oriented, no reproaches, no intent-guessing.
>
> Batching (PR-style; every item: ID, slide, type, observation, consequence, proposed patch, effort, confidence, delivery dependency, acceptance test, status):
>
> 1. **Release blockers** (factual conflict, unsupported public claim, broken media, privacy/licensing) — unlimited but rare; these outrank all aesthetics.
> 2. **≤3 high-impact changes**, ranked by audience benefit ÷ rework cost.
> 3. **≤3 clarifying questions** — only ones whose answers change a recommendation.
> 4. **One proposed patch set** (storyboard move, rewritten assertion, one-slide mockup).
> 5. **Optional polish** — collapsed checklist, never mixed with blockers.
> 6. **Preserve list** — 2–3 patterns that must not be disturbed (more useful than praise).
>
> Closure semantics: the PI should be able to reply `accept H1/H3, decline H2, answer Q1`. Delivery-dependent observations must say so and link to notes/rehearsal, not stand as unconditional findings.

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C10 Three global reviews:** thumbnails (rhythm/motifs); assertions-only (headlines must argue the talk by themselves); evidence-only (artifacts traceable, non-redundant, matched to claims). Plus a notes-only rehearsal check that narration extends rather than reads.

---

## Accessibility

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 7:

> **Layout & style extension** — host deck's tokens and semantic conventions, not its mistakes; bounded deviations for legibility/accessibility; new tokens documented and reused.

From **§3. Design rule 2**:

> *Test:* decisive text ≥ ~24 pt equivalent; provenance traceable from the notes.

From **§3. Design rule 4**:

> Keep dimmed context readable.

---

## Rehearsal

From **§2. The pipeline**:

> 9. **Rehearsal & rhetorical QA** — timing from rehearsal, not slide count. *PI required.*
>
> Two loops: evidence conflicts → back to 2–3; failed rehearsal → back to 3–6. Never patch a bad narrative with visual QA.

From **§3. Design rule 3**:

> ~20 projected wpm is a rehearsal trigger, not a release gate.

From **§3. Design rule 5**:

> **[T2] Time from rehearsal; classify every slide** core / optional module / backup / provenance. Cut from a pre-ranked list.

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C8 Pacing:** plot dwell × new-words × complexity × role across the deck; flag peaks and monotone runs; validate in rehearsal.
> - **C10** … Plus a notes-only rehearsal check that narration extends rather than reads.

---

## Handouts

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C9 Separate the live layer from the document layer** — notes/backup/repo docs carry provenance; the projection carries inference. Export a handout separately if needed.

---

## Backup Slides

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 4:

> Core additions go at their causal location; backups may be appended after a clear end marker; never dump core content as a trailing block.

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 10:

> **Packaging** — core deck + backups + media bundle + provenance map + change summary; per-slide PNG proofs so the PI can triage like a PR.

From **§3. Design rule 5**:

> **[T2] Time from rehearsal; classify every slide** core / optional module / backup / provenance. Cut from a pre-ranked list.

---

## Q&A

*(The guide does not contain an explicit Q&A section. The closest relevant lines are from the omission audit prompt in the referee task, which identifies Q&A/backup-slide strategy as something the guide missed — but that is the referee task framing, not guide text. No guide lines on Q&A exist to extract.)*

---

## Citations / Evidence Tiers

From **§3. Design rules** preamble:

> Evidence tiers from the literature pass (Edison iter2): **[T1]** = replicated experimental support (Mayer/CTML effect sizes d≈0.4–1.2; assertion–evidence studies); **[T2]** = consistent-with-theory craft knowledge.

From **§3. Design rule 8**:

> **[T2] Claim-dependent evidence schema.** Quantitative claims: unit, denominator, comparator, variability, scoring method — and don't confuse acceptance tolerance (±5 mg) with measurement uncertainty. Singular demos: provenance, operator, observation vs. inference, replication status. Agent self-report is a report; pair it with external verification (scale telemetry, video, human-held key) or narrow the claim and label it unverified.

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 2:

> **Evidence inventory** — index artifacts with source, date, actor, run ID, and what each does and does NOT establish. Flag conflicts (e.g., 0.9972 g vs 0.9956 g are different runs — never mix artifacts across runs on one slide). *PI resolves factual disputes.*

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 3:

> **Claim/beat selection** — claim–evidence ledger; reject beats redundant with the existing deck BEFORE layout; assign cut priority. *PI picks representative claims.*

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C2 Claim–evidence–payoff ledger:** no claim before its setup; no evidence without its "so what"; no unresolved promise at the close.

From **§6. The native-artifact library**:

> Rule: every evidence panel on a slide traces to one of these by path + commit + (for hardware runs) run ID.

From **§3. Design rule 2**:

> Verified transcription is allowed when crops can't reach room legibility — label it and keep a source thumbnail/pointer.

From **§5. Reviewing a hand-made deck**:

> 1. **Release blockers** (factual conflict, unsupported public claim, broken media, privacy/licensing) — unlimited but rare; these outrank all aesthetics.

---

## PowerPoint Mechanics

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 7:

> (PowerPoint web: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect; numeric size fields; masters not editable — see [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md).)

From **§7. Known mechanical constraints (PowerPoint for the web via automation)**:

> See [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md) for the full recipe. Highlights: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect (mandatory for verbatim text); numeric Shape ribbon fields for exact sizes; ≈92.3 px/in mapping for drag-positioning; slide masters are NOT editable in the web editor (use python-pptx + REST upload when the file is closed, or desktop PowerPoint); co-authoring works while the owner has the deck open; verify persistence against the re-downloaded blob, and verify *renders*, not just text.

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 10:

> per-slide PNG proofs so the PI can triage like a PR.

From **§3. Design rule 7**:

> **[T1 gates + T2 tests] Release gates:** no text/object overlap; no leftover placeholders; no off-slide objects (unless declared animation staging); safe margins; media plays on the delivery path; then re-render each slide and *look*; then role-specific cold-viewer checks (hook → orientation; claim → claim + focal evidence; demo → cue visibility; expert plot → entry point). Five-second/80% is craft, not validated — treat as a smoke test.

info.description:
Run code in a notebook cell and return the execution output.

This method allows running code in a new cell (append) or re-running
an existing cell with updated code.

Usage Examples:
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Creating example code") # Run code in new cell
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Modifying example code",
            idx=0) # Run code in existing cell at index 0

Error Recovery:
    When a cell fails with an error, you MUST fix it by calling run_cell
    with the corrected code and the SAME idx as the failed cell:

    run_cell("corrected_code", idx=3)  # Fix error in Cell #3

    The cell number is shown in the output prefix (e.g., "[Cell #3]").

Search the workspace or memory for information.

Spawns a lightweight sub-agent that can read files, grep, jq, and
run shell pipelines to find information in the workspace. Use this
instead of reading large files or exploring directories directly —
the sub-agent manages its own context so your context is not consumed.

What the sub-agent CAN do: list directories, read text and multimedia

You are a rigorous data analysis agent with deep expertise in statistics, data science, and quantitative methods. Your primary directive is to provide accurate, evidence-based analysis in Jupyter notebooks while maintaining the highest standards of scientific integrity.

## Core Principles

**Do not fabricate data for any reason**

You must never invent, simulate, or fabricate data under any circumstances. All analyses, visualizations, and interpretations must be directly derivable from the provided dataset or data correctly pulled in from external sources (eg. gene annotations, external databases). If you cannot access required data you must report this limitation and end the analysis. You must not subsample data without an analytical or technical purpose. If the data must be subsampled due to memory limitations or other technical constraints, this must be justified and reported.

**All analyses must demonstrate statistical rigor and methodological excellence**

Every analytical procedure must be statistically sound and suitable for the specific data type and research question being addressed. You should always consider and mention underlying statistical assumptions (normality, independence, homoscedasticity, etc.). You must check assumptions before applying statistical tests and report when assumptions are violated. You should use correct statistical terminology, notation, and precision in reporting. You must report relevant metrics: p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, test statistics, degrees of freedom. You should apply appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons when necessary. You must distinguish between correlation and causation, avoiding causal claims from observational data.

**Report the limitations of the data and your analysis**

If a request is beyond your capabilities or the scope of provided data, you must state this clearly and concisely. You should never attempt to answer questions requiring domain knowledge you do not possess or cannot acquire through use of tools such as external data sources or web search. That means it cannot access things like data repositories, blog posts, social media, company websites, and so on.
If your query requires access to such sources, consider using `e14c.web` (call `view_docs` to read more) as an alternative or complementary solution.

### Analysis

The `analysis` sub-agent can perform heavier computational tasks than you can.
It has access to a Python interpreter much like you do, but is given more CPUs and RAM.
Therefore, delegate any serious computational or data analysis tasks to it via `submit_task(agent_type="analysis")` (note that `"analysis"` is the default `agent_type`).
Also consider that once a script or library is written, the `analysis` agent can be called multiple times in parallel to execute the code with different parameterizations (e.g. a hyperparameter sweep).



### Molecules

The `molecules` sub-agent specializes in chemistry workflows and includes deeper chemistry-specific guidance and tooling. Delegate to `molecules` for any workflows that imply chemistry and cheminformatics. When the query involves chemical structures, reactions, metabolite identification, or similar tasks, look to the `molecules` sub-agent first before deciding to use other sub-agents.

### Data retrieval

The `data-retrieval` sub-agent is a specialized system for retrieving data from specific sources.
It has deeper support for a range of biological databases spanning expression, variants, structures, proteomics, pharmacology, and general data deposits — e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, PRIDE, KEGG, Zenodo, among others — and can also search sources beyond that set.
Use this agent when you know either:

1. a specific data source / dataset ID (e.g. GEO accession number)
2. or have narrowed things down to a small subset of data sources and need to perform a search against them (e.g. "find me RNA-seq datasets pertaining to ...")

### Artifact generation

The `artifact-generation` sub-agent produces file deliverables across formats — reports and papers (LaTeX/markdown); slide decks (`.pptx`); Word documents (`.docx`), spreadsheets (`.xlsx`); and infographics, schematics, and diagrams. Include the target format, allowed source task IDs/files/data entries, and any structural requirements in your dispatch query so the sub-agent routes correctly. It can delegate to `literature` for citation verification. Do not use `analysis` for artifact authoring — that agent's persona over-compresses and has no format-specific guidance.

## Dataset search and retrieval

For the specific task of dataset search and retrieval, there are multiple complementary strategies.
Decide which of the following (possibly multiple) are relevant for each search/retrieval task and apply accordingly.

- `e14c.web`: Directly search the web for broad sweeps when a relevant dataset could live across multiple sources (GitHub, Hugging Face, GEO, lab pages). - `submit_task(agent_type="data-retrieval")`: Targeted pull from a specific source (e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA) once you already know which source and roughly what you need from it (i.e. a specific dataset ID or targeted search query).

# Iteration 5 of 5: referee the final synthesis — the agent's operating guide for slide generation and review

## The loop so far
Iter1 adversarial critique reranked why 14 generated quote slides were cut from a CNMS
2026 talk (appended-prototype status + redundancy with natively-integrated beats +
rendering defects > pure style). Iter2 graded the design rules against the multimedia-
learning / assertion–evidence literature. Iter3 stress-tested the rubric into defeasible
purpose/default/exception/test form, produced a stage-gated pipeline with PI-judgment
gates, exposed a provenance trap in a redesign (mixing artifacts from two different dose
runs) and 10 deck-level cohesiveness rules. Iter4 produced a calibrated PR-style review
of the presented deck (blocker → ≤3 high-impact → ≤3 questions → patch set → optional
polish → preserve list, all with acceptance tests) plus a reusable two-pass review
checklist.

## The synthesized guide (referee this)

# Agent guide: generating and reviewing presentation slides for this lab

Synthesized 2026-08-13 (PR #176) from: the CNMS 2026 deck post-mortem
([cnms-2026-slide-style-analysis.md](cnms-2026-slide-style-analysis.md)), five Edison
Scientific critique iterations (artifacts + task IDs in
[`outputs/cnms-2026-slide-feedback/`](../outputs/cnms-2026-slide-feedback/)), and
Jean-luc Doumont's materials (three laws; "with each slide, convey one message — state
it verbally, develop it visually"; the Nature Masterclass exemplar decks). This is the
operating document future sessions should load before touching a deck.

## 0. The one-paragraph lesson

For CNMS 2026 I generated 14 verbatim-quote text slides; all 14 were cut. The corpus
mining and curation were used — the PI presented the same beats as **native artifacts**
(screen recordings of the real GitHub threads, phone video of hardware responding) —
but my rendering failed: appended as a trailing block instead of placed in the
narrative, redundant with beats already integrated, text-collision defects, and
document-styled where the deck's language is evidence-styled. Slide generation is a
pipeline with the PI's judgment gated in, not a rendering step at the end.

## 1. Before generating anything: the brief

Ask (one compact message, not an interview). Minimum viable: #1, #3, #4.

1. What should this audience believe/do at the end, in one sentence?
2. Who is in the room; what skepticism should the talk answer?
3. Hard speaking time and delivery mode (live demo? recording? offline fallback?).
4. Which beats are mandatory / expendable / confidential / non-negotiable?
5. Which deck is the canonical style reference; how much deviation is acceptable?
6. What evidentiary wording is acceptable (case study vs. validated performance claim)?

Propose defaults for unanswered items and display them before storyboarding.

## 2. The pipeline (stage → binding rules → PI gate)

1. **Brief contract** (above) — *PI required.*
2. **Evidence inventory** — index artifacts with source, date, actor, run ID, and what
   each does and does NOT establish. Flag conflicts (e.g., 0.9972 g vs 0.9956 g are
   different runs — never mix artifacts across runs on one slide). *PI resolves factual
   disputes.*
3. **Claim/beat selection** — claim–evidence ledger; reject beats redundant with the
   existing deck BEFORE layout; assign cut priority. *PI picks representative claims.*
4. **Narrative placement** — text storyboard; setup/payoff pairs; callbacks; optional
   modules with insertion/cut points. Core additions go at their causal location;
   backups may be appended after a clear end marker; never dump core content as a
   trailing block. *PI approves storyboard.*
5. **Form selection** — claim slide / process chain / comparison / demo cue / hook /
   transition / callback; static vs. build; what the speaker says that the slide
   doesn't. *PI confirms delivery-dependent choices.*
6. **Artifact preparation** — crop decisive region, mask chrome, annotate
   non-destructively; verified transcription only when a native crop can't pass
   room-legibility, always with a source pointer; never silently reconstruct plots or
   measurements.
7. **Layout & style extension** — host deck's tokens and semantic conventions, not its
   mistakes; bounded deviations for legibility/accessibility; new tokens documented and
   reused. (PowerPoint web: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect; numeric size fields;
   masters not editable — see [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md).)
8. **Render & technical QA** — gates below.
9. **Rehearsal & rhetorical QA** — timing from rehearsal, not slide count. *PI required.*
10. **Packaging** — core deck + backups + media bundle + provenance map + change
    summary; per-slide PNG proofs so the PI can triage like a PR.

Two loops: evidence conflicts → back to 2–3; failed rehearsal → back to 3–6. Never
patch a bad narrative with visual QA.

## 3. Design rules (defeasible defaults: purpose · default · exception · test)

Evidence tiers from the literature pass (Edison iter2): **[T1]** = replicated
experimental support (Mayer/CTML effect sizes d≈0.4–1.2; assertion–evidence studies);
**[T2]** = consistent-with-theory craft knowledge.

1. **[T1] One intended audience inference per slide/build.** Not "one content type" —
   an evidentiary chain (prompt → action → check) can be one inference. Analytic claims
   get a sentence assertion + visual evidence; demos get a what-to-watch-for cue;
   hooks/transitions may need neither. *Test:* name the inference; if you can't, the
   slide isn't ready.
2. **[T2] Prefer faithful extraction of native artifacts; preserve provenance and
   wording, not necessarily pixels.** Crop/enlarge/mask/annotate the real thing. The
   benefit runs through *clarity and annotation*, not authenticity per se (truthiness
   effect failed replication). Verified transcription is allowed when crops can't reach
   room legibility — label it and keep a source thumbnail/pointer. *Test:* decisive
   text ≥ ~24 pt equivalent; provenance traceable from the notes.
3. **[T1] Manage reading load, not word count.** Metric: *new, audience-directed
   readable words per exposure interval* (persistent labels and subordinate provenance
   don't recount). ~20 projected wpm is a rehearsal trigger, not a release gate.
   Complexity check besides words: focal regions, unfamiliar encodings, required
   comparisons. Quote slides: project the key phrase, let the audience read silently,
   then narrate commentary that *extends* (never reads) it.
4. **[T1] Build by emphasis only when order/suspense/correspondence matters.** Hold a
   skeleton constant, dim the past, highlight the current — but a static annotated
   chain or small multiples beats a mechanical 3-step build when experts can parse it
   at once. Keep dimmed context readable.
5. **[T2] Time from rehearsal; classify every slide** core / optional module / backup /
   provenance. Cut from a pre-ranked list.
6. **[T2] Match the host's stable tokens and semantics — not its defects.** Ask before
   introducing a conspicuous new motif.
7. **[T1 gates + T2 tests] Release gates:** no text/object overlap; no leftover
   placeholders; no off-slide objects (unless declared animation staging); safe
   margins; media plays on the delivery path; then re-render each slide and *look*;
   then role-specific cold-viewer checks (hook → orientation; claim → claim + focal
   evidence; demo → cue visibility; expert plot → entry point). Five-second/80% is
   craft, not validated — treat as a smoke test.
8. **[T2] Claim-dependent evidence schema.** Quantitative claims: unit, denominator,
   comparator, variability, scoring method — and don't confuse acceptance tolerance
   (±5 mg) with measurement uncertainty. Singular demos: provenance, operator,
   observation vs. inference, replication status. Agent self-report is a report;
   pair it with external verification (scale telemetry, video, human-held key) or
   narrow the claim and label it unverified.

## 4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules (checkable)

- **C1 Deck contract:** outcome sentence, opening tension, 3–5 section functions,
  closing answer, role of the framing device (e.g., Wizard-of-Oz). Every core slide
  maps to a function.
- **C2 Claim–evidence–payoff ledger:** no claim before its setup; no evidence without
  its "so what"; no unresolved promise at the close.
- **C3 Motif semantics:** each recurring motif means one thing (curtain = concealed
  human work; GitHub card = instruction/provenance). Audit thumbnails for one-off
  decorations and conflicting reuse.
- **C4 Repeated examples must advance state** (observe → act → close the loop →
  survive blinded evaluation); two adjacent examples with the same "new capability"
  answer → merge, cut, or turn one into a limitation.
- **C5 Section bridges:** last assertion of section N + first of N+1 must chain
  ("Remote action works; can we trust the result?").
- **C6 Entity/terminology identity:** stable names and visual identifiers; audit for
  synonym drift (Claude/agent/bot).
- **C7 Callbacks change meaning,** never just repeat imagery.
- **C8 Pacing:** plot dwell × new-words × complexity × role across the deck; flag
  peaks and monotone runs; validate in rehearsal.
- **C9 Separate the live layer from the document layer** — notes/backup/repo docs
  carry provenance; the projection carries inference. Export a handout separately if
  needed.
- **C10 Three global reviews:** thumbnails (rhythm/motifs); assertions-only (headlines
  must argue the talk by themselves); evidence-only (artifacts traceable,
  non-redundant, matched to claims). Plus a notes-only rehearsal check that narration
  extends rather than reads.

## 5. Reviewing a hand-made deck ("meaningful suggestions" mode)

Two passes: **narrative/evidence first**, visual polish only after structural decisions
land. Doumont feedback norms: observations as facts about the artifact/experience
("at 25% zoom the labels are unreadable to me"), future-oriented, no reproaches, no
intent-guessing.

Batching (PR-style; every item: ID, slide, type, observation, consequence, proposed
patch, effort, confidence, delivery dependency, acceptance test, status):

1. **Release blockers** (factual conflict, unsupported public claim, broken media,
   privacy/licensing) — unlimited but rare; these outrank all aesthetics.
2. **≤3 high-impact changes**, ranked by audience benefit ÷ rework cost.
3. **≤3 clarifying questions** — only ones whose answers change a recommendation.
4. **One proposed patch set** (storyboard move, rewritten assertion, one-slide mockup).
5. **Optional polish** — collapsed checklist, never mixed with blockers.
6. **Preserve list** — 2–3 patterns that must not be disturbed (more useful than
   praise).

Closure semantics: the PI should be able to reply `accept H1/H3, decline H2, answer
Q1`. Delivery-dependent observations must say so and link to notes/rehearsal, not
stand as unconditional findings.

## 6. The native-artifact library (what to build slides FROM)

~418 agent-committed media files across the three public repos (inventory method in
`outputs/cnms-2026-slide-feedback/`): camera stills (`byu-vcl/wireless-color-sensor/`,
`ot2-overhead-camera/`), CAD renders (`tensegrity-optimization/cad/`,
`powder-doser/design/`), BO plate previews (`tensegrity-optimization/bo/`), drop-test
figures (`data/drop-tests/`), dose telemetry (`powder-doser/data/pid-dose/`), prior
slide previews (`tensegrity-optimization/presentation/`) — plus the full comment corpus
(`data/cnms-2026-corpus/`) from which any comment card can be re-rendered at chosen
zoom, and 18 screen-recordings already embedded in the CNMS deck. Rule: every evidence
panel on a slide traces to one of these by path + commit + (for hardware runs) run ID.

## 7. Known mechanical constraints (PowerPoint for the web via automation)

See [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md) for the full recipe.
Highlights: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect (mandatory for verbatim text); numeric
Shape ribbon fields for exact sizes; ≈92.3 px/in mapping for drag-positioning; slide
masters are NOT editable in the web editor (use python-pptx + REST upload when the file
is closed, or desktop PowerPoint); co-authoring works while the owner has the deck
open; verify persistence against the re-downloaded blob, and verify *renders*, not just
text.


## Referee tasks
1. **Consistency audit:** find contradictions between guide sections, or places where
   the guide waters down a harder-won conclusion from iterations 1–4 (as summarized
   above). Quote the offending lines.
2. **Actionability audit:** which instructions would an autonomous agent be UNABLE to
   execute as written (unmeasurable, circular, requiring information it can't get)?
   Rewrite the three worst offenders.
3. **Omission audit:** what did iterations 1–4 establish that the guide fails to
   capture? What do presentation experts know that the whole loop still missed —
   e.g., anything from Doumont's actual delivery guidance, poster/handout distinctions,
   Q&A/backup-slide strategy, accessibility, non-native-English audiences?
4. **Failure-mode simulation:** simulate the guide against three future scenarios and
   report where it breaks: (a) 'make me 5 slides for a 10-min department seminar next
   week from the powder-doser repo'; (b) 'review my draft deck for the TMS 2027 talk'
   (a deck the agent has never seen, on CALPHAD work in a private repo); (c) 'add two
   slides on last month's results to my existing group-meeting deck while I'm at a
   conference' (no PI availability — the brief-contract gate cannot be satisfied).
5. **Verdict:** is this guide ready to be the lab's standing instruction for
   agent-generated slides? State the minimum changes for a yes.

## Required PI Gates

From **§2. The pipeline**:

> 1. **Brief contract** (above) — *PI required.*
> 2. **Evidence inventory** — … *PI resolves factual disputes.*
> 3. **Claim/beat selection** — … *PI picks representative claims.*

> 5. **Form selection** — … *PI confirms delivery-dependent choices.*
> 9. **Rehearsal & rhetorical QA** — timing from rehearsal, not slide count. *PI required.*

From **§0. The one-paragraph lesson**:

> Slide generation is a pipeline with the PI's judgment gated in, not a rendering step at the end.

From **§5. Reviewing a hand-made deck**:

> Closure semantics: the PI should be able to reply `accept H1/H3, decline H2, answer Q1`. Delivery-dependent observations must say so and link to notes/rehearsal, not stand as unconditional findings.

---

## Defaults for Missing Brief Information

From **§1. Before generating anything: the brief**:

> Ask (one compact message, not an interview). Minimum viable: #1, #3, #4.
>
> 1. What should this audience believe/do at the end, in one sentence?
> 2. Who is in the room; what skepticism should the talk answer?
> 3. Hard speaking time and delivery mode (live demo? recording? offline fallback?).
> 4. Which beats are mandatory / expendable / confidential / non-negotiable?
> 5. Which deck is the canonical style reference; how much deviation is acceptable?
> 6. What evidentiary wording is acceptable (case study vs. validated performance claim)?
>
> Propose defaults for unanswered items and display them before storyboarding.

---

## Review-Only versus Generation Procedures

From **§5. Reviewing a hand-made deck ("meaningful suggestions" mode)**:

> Two passes: **narrative/evidence first**, visual polish only after structural decisions land. Doumont feedback norms: observations as facts about the artifact/experience ("at 25% zoom the labels are unreadable to me"), future-oriented, no reproaches, no intent-guessing.
>
> Batching (PR-style; every item: ID, slide, type, observation, consequence, proposed patch, effort, confidence, delivery dependency, acceptance test, status):
>
> 1. **Release blockers** (factual conflict, unsupported public claim, broken media, privacy/licensing) — unlimited but rare; these outrank all aesthetics.
> 2. **≤3 high-impact changes**, ranked by audience benefit ÷ rework cost.
> 3. **≤3 clarifying questions** — only ones whose answers change a recommendation.
> 4. **One proposed patch set** (storyboard move, rewritten assertion, one-slide mockup).
> 5. **Optional polish** — collapsed checklist, never mixed with blockers.
> 6. **Preserve list** — 2–3 patterns that must not be disturbed (more useful than praise).
>
> Closure semantics: the PI should be able to reply `accept H1/H3, decline H2, answer Q1`. Delivery-dependent observations must say so and link to notes/rehearsal, not stand as unconditional findings.

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C10 Three global reviews:** thumbnails (rhythm/motifs); assertions-only (headlines must argue the talk by themselves); evidence-only (artifacts traceable, non-redundant, matched to claims). Plus a notes-only rehearsal check that narration extends rather than reads.

---

## Accessibility

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 7:

> **Layout & style extension** — host deck's tokens and semantic conventions, not its mistakes; bounded deviations for legibility/accessibility; new tokens documented and reused.

From **§3. Design rule 2**:

> *Test:* decisive text ≥ ~24 pt equivalent; provenance traceable from the notes.

From **§3. Design rule 4**:

> Keep dimmed context readable.

---

## Rehearsal

From **§2. The pipeline**:

> 9. **Rehearsal & rhetorical QA** — timing from rehearsal, not slide count. *PI required.*
>
> Two loops: evidence conflicts → back to 2–3; failed rehearsal → back to 3–6. Never patch a bad narrative with visual QA.

From **§3. Design rule 3**:

> ~20 projected wpm is a rehearsal trigger, not a release gate.

From **§3. Design rule 5**:

> **[T2] Time from rehearsal; classify every slide** core / optional module / backup / provenance. Cut from a pre-ranked list.

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C8 Pacing:** plot dwell × new-words × complexity × role across the deck; flag peaks and monotone runs; validate in rehearsal.
> - **C10** … Plus a notes-only rehearsal check that narration extends rather than reads.

---

## Handouts

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C9 Separate the live layer from the document layer** — notes/backup/repo docs carry provenance; the projection carries inference. Export a handout separately if needed.

---

## Backup Slides

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 4:

> Core additions go at their causal location; backups may be appended after a clear end marker; never dump core content as a trailing block.

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 10:

> **Packaging** — core deck + backups + media bundle + provenance map + change summary; per-slide PNG proofs so the PI can triage like a PR.

From **§3. Design rule 5**:

> **[T2] Time from rehearsal; classify every slide** core / optional module / backup / provenance. Cut from a pre-ranked list.

*(The guide does not contain an explicit Q&A section. The closest relevant lines are from the omission audit prompt in the referee task, which identifies Q&A/backup-slide strategy as something the guide missed — but that is the referee task framing, not guide text. No guide lines on Q&A exist to extract.)*

From **§3. Design rules** preamble:

> Evidence tiers from the literature pass (Edison iter2): **[T1]** = replicated experimental support (Mayer/CTML effect sizes d≈0.4–1.2; assertion–evidence studies); **[T2]** = consistent-with-theory craft knowledge.

From **§3. Design rule 8**:

> **[T2] Claim-dependent evidence schema.** Quantitative claims: unit, denominator, comparator, variability, scoring method — and don't confuse acceptance tolerance (±5 mg) with measurement uncertainty. Singular demos: provenance, operator, observation vs. inference, replication status. Agent self-report is a report; pair it with external verification (scale telemetry, video, human-held key) or narrow the claim and label it unverified.

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 2:

> **Evidence inventory** — index artifacts with source, date, actor, run ID, and what each does and does NOT establish. Flag conflicts (e.g., 0.9972 g vs 0.9956 g are different runs — never mix artifacts across runs on one slide). *PI resolves factual disputes.*

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 3:

> **Claim/beat selection** — claim–evidence ledger; reject beats redundant with the existing deck BEFORE layout; assign cut priority. *PI picks representative claims.*

From **§4. Deck-level cohesiveness rules**:

> - **C2 Claim–evidence–payoff ledger:** no claim before its setup; no evidence without its "so what"; no unresolved promise at the close.

From **§6. The native-artifact library**:

> Rule: every evidence panel on a slide traces to one of these by path + commit + (for hardware runs) run ID.

From **§3. Design rule 2**:

> Verified transcription is allowed when crops can't reach room legibility — label it and keep a source thumbnail/pointer.

From **§5. Reviewing a hand-made deck**:

> 1. **Release blockers** (factual conflict, unsupported public claim, broken media, privacy/licensing) — unlimited but rare; these outrank all aesthetics.

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 7:

> (PowerPoint web: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect; numeric size fields; masters not editable — see [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md).)

From **§7. Known mechanical constraints (PowerPoint for the web via automation)**:

> See [cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md](cnms-2026-onedrive-access.md) for the full recipe. Highlights: clipboard paste bypasses autocorrect (mandatory for verbatim text); numeric Shape ribbon fields for exact sizes; ≈92.3 px/in mapping for drag-positioning; slide masters are NOT editable in the web editor (use python-pptx + REST upload when the file is closed, or desktop PowerPoint); co-authoring works while the owner has the deck open; verify persistence against the re-downloaded blob, and verify *renders*, not just text.

From **§2. The pipeline**, stage 10:

> per-slide PNG proofs so the PI can triage like a PR.

From **§3. Design rule 7**:

> **[T1 gates + T2 tests] Release gates:** no text/object overlap; no leftover placeholders; no off-slide objects (unless declared animation staging); safe margins; media plays on the delivery path; then re-render each slide and *look*; then role-specific cold-viewer checks (hook → orientation; claim → claim + focal evidence; demo → cue visibility; expert plot → entry point). Five-second/80% is craft, not validated — treat as a smoke test.
